name: Corrected Calcium
description: Corrects a measured serum calcium level for low albumin, adding 0.8 mg/dL for every 1 g/dL that albumin falls below 4 g/dL. It estimates the calcium level that would be seen at normal albumin.
notes: Calcium is in mg/dL and albumin in g/dL, matching the 4.0 reference and 0.8 slope. It only adjusts for albumin binding and does not replace ionized calcium measurement.

name: Anion Gap
description: Calculates the serum anion gap by subtracting the measured anions chloride and bicarbonate from sodium. It reflects unmeasured anions and helps classify metabolic acidosis.
notes: All electrolytes are in mmol/L (equivalent to mEq/L for these monovalent ions). This version excludes potassium; a low albumin lowers the apparent gap and may need correction.

name: Anion Gap (with Potassium)
description: Calculates the anion gap including potassium, subtracting chloride and bicarbonate from the sum of sodium and potassium. Adding potassium raises the gap slightly versus the sodium-only version.
notes: All values in mmol/L. Because potassium is included, the normal reference range is a few units higher than for the potassium-free anion gap.

name: Shock Index
description: Computes the shock index as heart rate divided by systolic blood pressure. Higher values indicate hemodynamic instability, with a normal range of roughly 0.5 to 0.7.
notes: Heart rate is in beats per minute and systolic pressure in mmHg; the ratio is dimensionless. It is a screening trend rather than a diagnosis and can be skewed by medications affecting heart rate.

name: QTc (Bazett)
description: Corrects the QT interval for heart rate using Bazett's formula, dividing the QT interval by the square root of the RR interval. It normalizes QT to a heart rate of 60 beats per minute.
notes: QT and RR are both in seconds, so QTc is also in seconds. Bazett over-corrects at fast heart rates and under-corrects at slow rates compared with other formulas.

name: QTc (Fridericia)
description: Corrects the QT interval for heart rate using Fridericia's formula, dividing the QT interval by the cube root of the RR interval. It normalizes QT and is more accurate than Bazett at extreme heart rates.
notes: QT and RR are in seconds, giving QTc in seconds. The cube-root correction reduces the rate dependence errors seen with Bazett at very fast or slow rates.

name: Parkland Formula (Burn Fluid)
description: Estimates the total crystalloid fluid needed in the first 24 hours after a burn by the Parkland formula, as 4 mL times body weight times the percent of body surface burned. It guides burn resuscitation.
notes: Weight in kg and burned area as a percent of total body surface area. Half the total is given over the first 8 hours from the time of injury and the rest over the next 16 hours.

name: Sodium Deficit
description: Estimates the amount of sodium needed to raise serum sodium to a target, as the sodium gap times total body water (0.6 times weight). It guides correction of hyponatremia.
notes: Sodium values in mmol/L and weight in kg; the 0.6 factor is total body water fraction and is lower in women and the elderly. Correct sodium slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.

name: Free Water Deficit
description: Estimates the free water deficit in hypernatremia, as total body water (0.6 times weight) times the fractional excess of serum sodium above the normal 140. The result is the water volume needed to normalize sodium.
notes: Weight in kg and sodium in mmol/L; the result is in liters. The 0.6 body water fraction should be reduced for women and the elderly, and sodium should be lowered gradually.

name: Serum Osmolality
description: Calculates estimated serum osmolality from sodium, glucose, and BUN, doubling sodium and adding glucose over 18 and BUN over 2.8. It approximates the osmotic concentration of blood.
notes: Sodium in mmol/L, glucose and BUN in mg/dL; the divisors convert those to mmol/L contributions. Comparing this to measured osmolality gives the osmolal gap.

name: Effective Serum Osmolality
description: Calculates effective serum osmolality (tonicity) from sodium and glucose, doubling sodium and adding glucose over 18, omitting urea. It reflects the osmoles that actually drive water shifts across cell membranes.
notes: Sodium in mmol/L and glucose in mg/dL. Urea is excluded because it crosses membranes freely and does not contribute to effective osmotic force.

name: Corrected Sodium for Hyperglycemia
description: Corrects measured sodium for hyperglycemia, adding 1.6 mmol/L for each 100 mg/dL that glucose exceeds 100. It estimates the true sodium once the osmotic dilution from high glucose is accounted for.
notes: Sodium in mmol/L and glucose in mg/dL. The 1.6 factor is a common convention; some use 2.4, which yields a higher corrected value at very high glucose.

name: Maintenance Fluids (Holliday-Segar, >20kg)
description: Computes daily maintenance fluid requirement for patients over 20 kg by the Holliday-Segar method, as 1500 mL plus 20 mL for each kilogram above 20. The result is the 24-hour fluid volume.
notes: Weight in kg and this branch applies only above 20 kg; lower weights use different per-kg rates. It estimates basal maintenance needs and does not include deficit or ongoing losses.

name: Alveolar Gas Equation (PAO2)
description: Estimates the alveolar partial pressure of oxygen by the alveolar gas equation, as inspired oxygen fraction times (atmospheric pressure minus water vapor pressure 47) minus arterial CO2 over the respiratory quotient 0.8. It gives ideal alveolar PO2.
notes: FiO2 is a fraction (0.21 for room air), pressures in mmHg, and 47 mmHg is water vapor at body temperature. The 0.8 respiratory quotient is an assumption that varies with diet and metabolism.

name: A-a Oxygen Gradient
description: Computes the alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient by subtracting the measured arterial PaO2 from the alveolar PO2 given by the alveolar gas equation. A widened gradient indicates a problem with gas exchange.
notes: FiO2 is a fraction, all pressures in mmHg. The normal gradient rises with age and with higher FiO2, so interpret the value against age-adjusted expectations.

name: Estimated Blood Volume
description: Estimates total blood volume by multiplying body weight by an average blood volume per kilogram. It approximates circulating blood volume for transfusion and blood loss calculations.
notes: Weight in kg and blood volume per kg in mL/kg, roughly 70 for adult men, 65 for women, and higher for neonates. Select the per-kg value appropriate to the patient group.

name: Pack-Years
description: Calculates smoking exposure in pack-years by multiplying the number of packs smoked per day by the number of years smoked. One pack-year equals a pack a day for a year.
notes: Packs per day assumes 20 cigarettes per pack; convert cigarettes per day by dividing by 20. For varying habits, sum pack-years over each period separately.

name: Fractional Excretion of Sodium (FENa)
description: Computes the fractional excretion of sodium as a percent, from urine and serum sodium and creatinine, as (urine sodium times serum creatinine) over (serum sodium times urine creatinine) times 100. It helps distinguish causes of acute kidney injury.
notes: Sodium values and creatinine values must each be in matching units so they cancel. A value below 1% suggests prerenal azotemia; recent diuretic use invalidates the interpretation.

name: Transferrin Saturation
description: Calculates transferrin saturation as a percent, dividing serum iron by total iron-binding capacity and multiplying by 100. It shows what fraction of iron-binding sites are occupied by iron.
notes: Serum iron and TIBC must share the same unit (here ug/dL) so they cancel. Low values suggest iron deficiency and high values iron overload.

name: Absolute Neutrophil Count
description: Calculates the absolute neutrophil count from the white cell count and the combined percentage of segmented and band neutrophils. It quantifies infection-fighting neutrophils and gauges neutropenia risk.
notes: WBC in cells per microliter and the neutrophil and band values as percentages summed then divided by 100. An ANC below 500 indicates severe neutropenia with high infection risk.

name: Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV)
description: Calculates the mean corpuscular volume, the average size of a red blood cell, as hematocrit times 10 divided by the red cell count. The result in femtoliters classifies anemias by cell size.
notes: Hematocrit as a percent and RBC count in millions per microliter; the factor 10 makes the units work out to femtoliters. Low MCV means microcytic and high means macrocytic anemia.

name: Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin (MCH)
description: Calculates the mean corpuscular hemoglobin, the average mass of hemoglobin per red blood cell, as hemoglobin times 10 divided by the red cell count. The result in picograms reflects the hemoglobin content of each cell.
notes: Hemoglobin in g/dL and RBC count in millions per microliter; the factor 10 yields picograms. MCH tends to parallel MCV and is low in iron deficiency.

name: Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Conc. (MCHC)
description: Calculates the mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration, the hemoglobin concentration within red cells, as hemoglobin divided by hematocrit times 100. It indicates how densely packed hemoglobin is in the cells.
notes: Hemoglobin in g/dL and hematocrit as a percent give a result in g/dL. Low MCHC is hypochromic; abnormally high values can signal spherocytosis or a lab measurement error.

name: Corrected Reticulocyte Count
description: Corrects the reticulocyte percentage for the degree of anemia, multiplying it by the patient's hematocrit divided by a normal hematocrit of 45. It gives a truer picture of bone marrow red cell production.
notes: Reticulocyte and hematocrit both as percents; 45 is the assumed normal hematocrit. The correction prevents overestimating reticulocytosis when the total red cell mass is low.

name: Henderson-Hasselbalch pH
description: Calculates blood pH by the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, as 6.1 plus the base-10 logarithm of bicarbonate divided by dissolved CO2 (0.03 times pCO2). It links the bicarbonate buffer system to blood acidity.
notes: Bicarbonate in mmol/L and pCO2 in mmHg; 6.1 is the pKa of carbonic acid and 0.03 the CO2 solubility factor. It describes the carbonic acid-bicarbonate buffer only.

name: Cardiac Output (Fick)
description: Estimates cardiac output using the Fick principle, dividing whole-body oxygen consumption by the arterial-venous oxygen content difference. That difference is computed from hemoglobin, its oxygen-carrying capacity (1.34 mL O2 per gram), and the arterial minus venous saturations.
notes: Saturations are entered as percentages; the factor 10 converts g/dL to g/L. Result is in L/min. Ignores dissolved oxygen, so it slightly underestimates true content.

name: Mean Arterial Pressure (from Cardiac Output and Peripheral Resistance)
description: Estimates mean arterial pressure (MAP) as the product of cardiac output (CO) and total peripheral resistance (TPR), analogous to Ohm's law (V = I×R) applied to the circulatory system. This relationship underlies how changes in cardiac output or vascular resistance affect blood pressure.
notes: Assumes central venous pressure is negligible (approximately 0 mmHg), which is normally a reasonable approximation; results should be interpreted alongside clinical context, as normal MAP is typically 70-100 mmHg.

name: Total Peripheral Resistance (from MAP and Cardiac Output)
description: Calculates total peripheral resistance (TPR), the resistance the systemic circulation offers to blood flow, by dividing mean arterial pressure (MAP) by cardiac output (CO). This is the inverse relationship of the MAP = CO × TPR equation, analogous to Ohm's law (R = V/I).
notes: Assumes central venous pressure is negligible; elevated TPR is a hallmark of conditions such as essential hypertension, while decreased TPR is seen in states like septic shock.

name: Cardiac Output
description: Calculates cardiac output, the volume of blood the heart pumps per minute, by multiplying heart rate by stroke volume. The result is expressed in milliliters per minute.
notes: Heart rate is beats per minute and stroke volume the blood ejected per beat, so their product is volume per minute. Divide by 1000 to convert the result to liters per minute.

name: Stroke Volume
description: Calculates stroke volume, the amount of blood ejected by the heart in one beat, as the end-diastolic volume minus the end-systolic volume. It represents the blood the ventricle pumps out each contraction.
notes: Both volumes must be in the same unit (mL), and end-diastolic should exceed end-systolic for a positive result. It reflects one ventricle, typically the left.

name: Ejection Fraction
description: Calculates the ejection fraction, the percentage of end-diastolic blood the heart ejects per beat, as (end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume) divided by end-diastolic volume times 100. It is a key measure of cardiac pumping efficiency.
notes: Both volumes must use the same unit; the result is a percentage. A normal left-ventricular ejection fraction is roughly 55 to 70 percent, and low values indicate impaired function.

name: Cardiac Index
description: Calculates the cardiac index by dividing cardiac output by body surface area, normalizing heart pumping to body size. It allows fair comparison of cardiac performance between individuals of different sizes.
notes: Cardiac output is in liters per minute and body surface area in square meters, giving L/min/m². A normal resting range is about 2.5 to 4.0.

name: Mean Arterial Pressure
description: Estimates mean arterial pressure, the average pressure driving blood through the circulation over one cardiac cycle, as diastolic pressure plus one third of the pulse pressure (systolic minus diastolic). It weights diastole more because it lasts longer.
notes: Both pressures are in mmHg; the one-third factor is an approximation valid at resting heart rates and becomes less accurate at high rates. A typical normal value is around 70 to 100 mmHg.

name: Pulse Pressure
description: Calculates pulse pressure, the difference between systolic and diastolic blood pressure. It reflects the force the heart generates with each beat and the stiffness of the arteries.
notes: Both pressures are in mmHg. A normal pulse pressure is roughly 40 mmHg; widened or narrowed values can signal arterial stiffness or reduced stroke volume.

name: Respiratory Quotient
description: Calculates the respiratory quotient by dividing the volume of carbon dioxide produced by the volume of oxygen consumed. This dimensionless ratio indicates which fuel type the body is primarily metabolizing.
notes: Both gas volumes must share units so the result is a pure ratio; values near 1.0 suggest carbohydrate use, around 0.7 fat use. Measure both over the same interval.

name: Arterial Oxygen Content (CaO2)
description: Calculates arterial oxygen content in blood, summing oxygen bound to hemoglobin (1.34 times hemoglobin times fractional saturation) and oxygen dissolved in plasma (0.003 times partial pressure). The result is milliliters of oxygen per deciliter of blood.
notes: Saturation is entered as a percent and internally divided by 100; the dissolved term is small but included. The 1.34 constant is oxygen bound per gram of hemoglobin (some texts use 1.36 or 1.39).

name: Oxygen Delivery (DO2)
description: Calculates total oxygen delivery to the tissues per minute, multiplying cardiac output by arterial oxygen content, with a factor of 10 for unit conversion. It represents the amount of oxygen the circulation supplies each minute.
notes: The factor of 10 converts cardiac output in L/min and content in mL/dL into mL/min; keep those input units. It measures oxygen supplied, not oxygen actually consumed.

name: Oxygen Consumption (Fick Principle)
description: Calculates whole-body oxygen consumption using the Fick principle, multiplying cardiac output by the arterial minus venous oxygen content difference, times 10 for unit conversion. It gives the oxygen the tissues actually extract per minute.
notes: The factor of 10 matches cardiac output in L/min with content in mL/dL to give mL/min. Arterial content should exceed venous content; the difference is the extracted oxygen.

name: Creatinine Clearance (Cockcroft-Gault, Male)
description: Estimates creatinine clearance in adult males using the Cockcroft-Gault equation: (140 minus age) times body weight divided by (72 times serum creatinine). It approximates kidney filtration function in mL/min.
notes: This is the male form; females multiply the result by 0.85. Age is in years, weight in kg, and serum creatinine in mg/dL; it is an estimate, less reliable at extremes of body size.

name: Renal Clearance
description: Calculates renal clearance of a substance, the volume of plasma cleared of it per minute, as urine concentration times urine flow rate divided by plasma concentration. It measures how effectively the kidneys remove that substance.
notes: Urine and plasma concentrations must use the same units so they cancel, leaving the flow-rate unit (mL/min). Using an ideal marker such as inulin makes clearance equal glomerular filtration rate.

name: Minute Ventilation
description: Calculates minute ventilation, the total volume of air moved in and out of the lungs per minute, by multiplying respiratory rate by tidal volume. The result is in milliliters per minute.
notes: Respiratory rate is breaths per minute and tidal volume the air per breath, so their product is volume per minute. This total includes dead-space air, unlike alveolar ventilation.

name: Alveolar Ventilation
description: Calculates alveolar ventilation, the volume of fresh air reaching the gas-exchanging alveoli per minute, as (tidal volume minus dead space volume) times respiratory rate. It reflects the air that actually participates in gas exchange.
notes: Subtracting dead space distinguishes this from minute ventilation, which does not. Volumes are in mL and rate in breaths per minute; tidal volume must exceed dead space.

name: Corrected QT Interval (Bazett)
description: Corrects the measured ECG QT interval for heart rate using Bazett's formula, dividing QT by the square root of the RR interval. It normalizes QT to a heart rate of 60 bpm so intervals can be compared across rates.
notes: QT is in milliseconds but RR must be in seconds. Bazett over-corrects at fast rates and under-corrects at slow rates; Fridericia or other formulas are preferred outside 60-100 bpm.

name: Corrected QT Interval (Fridericia)
description: Corrects the ECG QT interval for heart rate using Fridericia's formula, dividing QT by the cube root of the RR interval. It normalizes QT to 60 bpm and is more reliable than Bazett at extreme heart rates.
notes: QT is in milliseconds and RR in seconds. The cube-root correction reduces rate dependence but still assumes a stable, regular rhythm; irregular rhythms make any single RR unrepresentative.

name: Corrected Serum Calcium (Albumin)
description: Adjusts measured serum calcium for low albumin, adding 0.8 mg/dL for every 1 g/dL that albumin falls below 4 g/dL. It estimates the calcium level that would be seen at a normal albumin, since much calcium is albumin-bound.
notes: Calcium is in mg/dL and albumin in g/dL; the 4 g/dL reference and 0.8 factor are unit-specific. The correction is an approximation and unreliable in critical illness or altered protein binding; ionized calcium is definitive.

name: Calculated Serum Osmolality
description: Estimates serum osmolality from its major osmotically active solutes: twice the sodium (for accompanying anions) plus glucose and blood urea nitrogen converted from mg/dL to mmol/L by dividing by 18 and 2.8. It approximates measured osmolality.
notes: Sodium is in mEq/L, glucose and BUN in mg/dL; the divisors 18 and 2.8 are mg/dL-specific conversions. A large gap between this estimate and measured osmolality suggests unmeasured osmoles such as alcohols.

name: Winter's Formula (Expected pCO2)
description: Predicts the expected arterial pCO2 for adequate respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis, as 1.5 times the bicarbonate plus 8 mmHg. Comparing measured pCO2 to this value detects a superimposed respiratory disorder.
notes: Bicarbonate is in mEq/L and the result in mmHg (typically +/- 2). A measured pCO2 above the predicted range indicates concurrent respiratory acidosis; below it, respiratory alkalosis. Valid only for metabolic acidosis.

name: eGFR (CKD-EPI 2021, Race-Free)
description: Estimates glomerular filtration rate from serum creatinine, age and sex with the 2021 CKD-EPI equation, which omits race.
notes: Below 60 for three months or more indicates chronic kidney disease.

name: MELD Score
description: Gives the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score predicting 3-month mortality (values below 1 are set to 1, creatinine capped at 4).
notes: Transplant programmes now often use MELD-Na or MELD 3.0; round the result to a whole number.

name: FIB-4 Index
description: Estimates liver fibrosis from age, liver enzymes and platelets (Sterling 2006).
notes: Below 1.3 makes advanced fibrosis unlikely; above 2.67 likely.

name: APRI (AST-to-Platelet Ratio Index)
description: Gives a simple non-invasive marker of liver fibrosis.
notes: Above about 1.5 suggests significant fibrosis.

name: HOMA-IR (Insulin Resistance)
description: Estimates insulin resistance from fasting glucose and insulin (Matthews 1985).
notes: Above about 2.5 is often taken as insulin resistance.

name: HOMA-β (Beta-Cell Function)
description: Estimates pancreatic beta-cell function from fasting glucose and insulin.
notes: 100 % is the reference of a healthy young adult.

name: QUICKI (Insulin Sensitivity Index)
description: Gives the quantitative insulin sensitivity check index (Katz 2000); lower values mean more insulin resistance.
notes: Healthy adults are around 0.37.

name: Estimated Average Glucose from HbA1c
description: Converts HbA1c into the average blood glucose over about three months (ADAG study, Nathan 2008).
notes: Divide by 18 for mmol/L.

name: HbA1c: NGSP (%) to IFCC (mmol/mol)
description: Converts HbA1c from the DCCT/NGSP percentage to the IFCC unit used in much of the world.
notes: 6.5 % (diabetes threshold) = 48 mmol/mol.

name: LDL Cholesterol (Friedewald)
description: Estimates LDL cholesterol from a standard lipid panel (Friedewald 1972).
notes: Invalid when triglycerides exceed 400 mg/dL; use TG/2.2 for mmol/L.

name: LDL Cholesterol (Sampson / NIH Equation)
description: Estimates LDL cholesterol more accurately than Friedewald at high triglycerides or low LDL (Sampson et al. 2020).
notes: Valid up to triglycerides of about 800 mg/dL.

name: Albumin-Corrected Anion Gap
description: Corrects the anion gap for low albumin, which otherwise hides a raised gap (Figge 1998).
notes: Each 1 g/dL fall in albumin lowers the gap by about 2.5.

name: Delta Ratio (Delta Gap)
description: Compares the rise in anion gap with the fall in bicarbonate to detect mixed acid–base disorders.
notes: 1–2 pure high-gap acidosis; below 1 added normal-gap acidosis; above 2 added metabolic alkalosis.

name: Bicarbonate Deficit
description: Estimates the bicarbonate needed to restore normal levels, using a distribution volume of about half body weight.
notes: Usually only part is replaced, with repeated measurements.

name: PaO₂/FiO₂ Ratio
description: Gives the oxygenation ratio used to grade ARDS (Berlin definition): ≤ 300 mild, ≤ 200 moderate, ≤ 100 severe.
notes: Measured with PEEP of at least 5 cmH₂O.

name: Oxygenation Index
description: Combines oxygen need and ventilator pressure into one severity score, especially in neonatal and paediatric care.
notes: Above about 25–40 may prompt ECMO consideration.

name: Rapid Shallow Breathing Index
description: Predicts success of weaning from a ventilator (Yang and Tobin 1991): below about 105 favours extubation.
notes: Measured during a spontaneous breathing trial.

name: Static Respiratory Compliance
description: Gives the stiffness of the lungs and chest wall during a breath hold on a ventilator.
notes: Normal is about 50–100; ARDS often below 40.

name: Driving Pressure
description: Gives the pressure that inflates the lungs with each breath; values above about 15 cmH₂O are linked to higher mortality in ARDS (Amato 2015).
notes: Equals tidal volume divided by compliance.

name: Physiological Dead Space Fraction (Bohr–Enghoff)
description: Gives the fraction of each breath that does not take part in gas exchange.
notes: Normal is about 0.2–0.35; raised in pulmonary embolism and ARDS.

name: Protective Tidal Volume (ARDSNet)

variables.label: Target mL per kg predicted body weight

description: Gives a lung-protective tidal volume from predicted body weight (ARDS Network 2000).
notes: Use height, not actual weight.

name: Cerebral Perfusion Pressure
description: Gives the pressure driving blood flow to the brain; guidelines target about 60–70 mmHg in traumatic brain injury.
notes: Raised intracranial pressure cuts it directly.

name: Systemic Vascular Resistance
description: Gives the resistance of the systemic circulation in the units used at the bedside (normal about 800–1200).
notes: High in cardiogenic shock, low in sepsis.

name: Pulmonary Vascular Resistance
description: Gives the resistance of the lung circulation; above about 240 dyn·s/cm⁵ (3 Wood units) suggests pulmonary vascular disease.
notes: Divide by 80 for Wood units.

name: Cardiac Power Output
description: Gives the heart's hydraulic power; below about 0.6 W is the strongest predictor of death in cardiogenic shock (Fincke 2004).
notes: Normal at rest is about 1 W.

name: Ankle–Brachial Index
description: Compares ankle and arm blood pressure to screen for peripheral artery disease: 0.9 or below is abnormal.
notes: Above 1.4 suggests stiff, calcified arteries.

name: QTc (Framingham)
description: Corrects the QT interval for heart rate with the linear Framingham formula (Sagie 1992), less biased than Bazett at high heart rates.
notes: Above about 450 ms (men) or 460 ms (women) is prolonged.

name: QTc (Hodges)
description: Corrects the QT interval for heart rate with the linear Hodges formula.
notes: Performs well across a wide range of heart rates.

name: Modified Shock Index
description: Divides heart rate by mean arterial pressure; above about 1.3 predicts higher mortality in emergencies.
notes: Uses MAP instead of systolic pressure.

name: CHA₂DS₂-VASc Score
expression: chf + htn + if(age >= 75, 2, if(age >= 65, 1, 0)) + dm + 2 * stk + vasc + fem
description: Scores stroke risk in atrial fibrillation (Lip 2010) to guide anticoagulation.
notes: Anticoagulation is generally recommended from 2 (men) or 3 (women).

name: Maintenance Fluid Rate (4-2-1 Rule, Any Weight)
description: Gives the hourly maintenance fluid rate by the Holliday–Segar "4-2-1" rule for any body weight.
notes: 4 mL/kg for the first 10 kg, 2 for the next 10, then 1.

name: Estimated Child Weight (APLS)
description: Estimates a child's weight from age for emergency drug dosing when weighing is impossible (APLS).
notes: Newer APLS formulas split by age band; use a measured or tape-based weight when possible.

name: Paediatric Endotracheal Tube Size (Uncuffed)
description: Estimates the internal diameter of an uncuffed tracheal tube for a child; subtract 0.5 for cuffed tubes.
notes: Have sizes 0.5 mm above and below ready.

name: Adjusted Body Weight
description: Gives a dosing weight for obese patients between ideal and actual weight, used for aminoglycosides and nutrition.
notes: The factor 0.4 is conventional; some drugs use 0.3.

name: Ideal Body Weight (Robinson)
description: Estimates ideal body weight from height (Robinson 1983): 52 kg (men) or 49 kg (women) at 5 ft plus a set amount per inch.
notes: Several formulas exist (Devine, Hamwi, Miller); results differ by a few kg.

name: Total Body Water (Watson)
description: Estimates total body water from age, height, weight and sex (Watson 1980), used for dialysis dosing (V in Kt/V).
notes: About 60 % of body weight in lean men.

name: Blood Volume (Nadler, Female)
description: Estimates total blood volume of a woman from height and weight (Nadler 1962).
notes: The male formula uses 0.3669, 0.03219 and 0.6041.

name: Body Fat (US Navy, Female)
description: Estimates a woman's body-fat percentage from tape measurements (US Navy method, Hodgdon and Beckett 1984).
notes: Measurements are in inches.

name: Relative Fat Mass (RFM)
description: Estimates body-fat percentage from height and waist alone (Woolcott and Bergman 2018), more accurate than BMI.
notes: Use the same units for height and waist.

name: A Body Shape Index (ABSI)
description: Gives waist size adjusted for BMI and height (Krakauer 2012); higher values predict mortality independently of BMI.
notes: Typical adult values are around 0.08.

name: Ponderal Index
description: Gives weight over height cubed, better than BMI for very short or tall people and for newborns.
notes: Newborns are typically 20–30 kg/m³.

name: Fat-Free Mass Index (Normalised)
description: Gives lean mass relative to height, normalised to 1.8 m (Kouri 1995); used to judge muscularity.
notes: Natural athletes rarely exceed about 25.

name: Dialysis Dose Kt/V (Daugirdas)
description: Gives the single-pool Kt/V dialysis adequacy from blood urea before and after a session (Daugirdas 1993).
notes: Guidelines target at least 1.2 per session for thrice-weekly haemodialysis.

name: Urea Reduction Ratio
description: Gives the percentage fall in blood urea during a dialysis session; 65 % or more is considered adequate.
notes: Simpler than Kt/V but ignores ultrafiltration.

name: Oxygen Cylinder Duration
description: Gives how long an oxygen cylinder lasts at a given flow.
notes: Keep a safety reserve of about 200 psi.

name: Approximate FiO₂ on Nasal Cannula
description: Estimates the inspired oxygen fraction delivered by a nasal cannula: about 4 % per litre per minute above room air.
notes: Only a rule of thumb; breathing pattern changes it.

name: Estimated Fetal Weight (Hadlock, AC and FL)
description: Estimates fetal weight from ultrasound abdominal circumference and femur length (Hadlock 1985).
notes: Error is typically ±10–15 %.

name: Corrected Age for Prematurity
description: Gives a premature baby's age from the due date, used to judge development until about two years.
notes: Chronological age minus the weeks born early.

name: Glucose: mg/dL to mmol/L
description: Converts blood glucose from US (mg/dL) to SI (mmol/L) units.
notes: Fasting 126 mg/dL = 7.0 mmol/L (diabetes threshold).

name: Cholesterol: mg/dL to mmol/L
description: Converts total, LDL or HDL cholesterol from mg/dL to mmol/L.
notes: 200 mg/dL ≈ 5.17 mmol/L.

name: Triglycerides: mg/dL to mmol/L
description: Converts triglycerides from mg/dL to mmol/L.
notes: 150 mg/dL ≈ 1.69 mmol/L.

name: Creatinine: µmol/L to mg/dL
description: Converts serum creatinine from SI units (µmol/L) to mg/dL.
notes: 1 mg/dL = 88.42 µmol/L.

name: Calcium: mg/dL to mmol/L
description: Converts serum calcium from mg/dL to mmol/L.
notes: Normal is about 2.2–2.6 mmol/L.

name: Urea Nitrogen (BUN) to Urea
description: Converts US blood urea nitrogen (mg/dL) into urea in mmol/L as reported in most other countries.
notes: For urea in mg/dL multiply BUN by 2.14.

name: Haemoglobin: g/dL to mmol/L
description: Converts haemoglobin from g/dL to mmol/L (monomer), as reported in the Netherlands and some other countries.
notes: Multiply g/dL by 10 for g/L.

name: Vitamin D: ng/mL to nmol/L
description: Converts 25-hydroxyvitamin D from ng/mL to nmol/L.
notes: 30 ng/mL ≈ 75 nmol/L.

name: Drug Level: mg/L to µmol/L
description: Converts a drug or metabolite concentration from mass units to molar units.
notes: mg/L is the same as µg/mL.

name: INR from Prothrombin Time
description: Standardises a prothrombin time across laboratories into the International Normalised Ratio (WHO).
notes: Warfarin targets are usually INR 2–3.

name: Reticulocyte Production Index

variables.label: Maturation factor (1.0 at Hct 45, 1.5 at 35, 2.0 at 25, 2.5 at 15)

description: Adjusts the reticulocyte count for anaemia and early release; above 2–3 suggests the marrow is responding (blood loss or haemolysis).
notes: Below 2 with anaemia suggests underproduction.

name: WBC Corrected for Nucleated Red Cells
description: Corrects an automated white-cell count that also counted nucleated red cells, as in newborns and severe anaemia.
notes: Modern analysers often correct automatically.

name: Serum–Ascites Albumin Gradient
description: Classifies ascites: 1.1 g/dL or more indicates portal hypertension (e.g. cirrhosis); below 1.1 other causes.
notes: Measure both samples the same day.

name: Urine Anion Gap
description: Helps tell renal from gut causes of normal-gap metabolic acidosis: negative values point to diarrhoea, positive to renal tubular acidosis.
notes: Reflects urine ammonium indirectly.

name: Transtubular Potassium Gradient
description: Estimates potassium secretion in the distal nephron; below about 7 with high potassium suggests low aldosterone effect.
notes: Valid only when urine osmolality exceeds plasma osmolality.

name: Fractional Excretion of Urea
description: Distinguishes pre-renal from intrinsic kidney injury, and still works in patients on diuretics: below 35 % suggests pre-renal.
notes: An alternative to FENa for diuretic users.

name: Electrolyte-Free Water Clearance
description: Gives the volume of electrolyte-free water the kidneys excrete; negative values mean water is retained, lowering sodium.
notes: Guides fluid restriction in hyponatraemia.

name: Atherogenic Index of Plasma
description: Gives log(TG/HDL) in mmol/L, a marker of small dense LDL and cardiovascular risk.
notes: Below 0.11 low risk, above 0.21 high risk (commonly used cut-offs).

name: Triglyceride–Glucose (TyG) Index
description: Gives a simple surrogate of insulin resistance from fasting triglycerides and glucose (Simental-Mendía 2008).
notes: Values above about 8.5–8.8 suggest insulin resistance.

name: Pressure Gradient from Doppler Velocity (Simplified Bernoulli)
description: Converts a Doppler blood-flow velocity into the pressure drop across a valve or narrowing.
notes: A 4 m/s aortic jet means a 64 mmHg peak gradient (severe stenosis).

name: Right Ventricular Systolic Pressure
description: Estimates pulmonary artery systolic pressure from the tricuspid regurgitant jet on echocardiography.
notes: Above about 35–40 mmHg suggests pulmonary hypertension.

name: Aortic Valve Area (Continuity Equation)
description: Gives the aortic valve opening area from the continuity of flow through the outflow tract and the valve.
notes: Below 1.0 cm² is severe aortic stenosis.

name: Left Ventricular Mass (Devereux)
description: Estimates left ventricular mass from M-mode or 2-D echo measurements (ASE-corrected Devereux formula).
notes: Index to body surface area to diagnose hypertrophy.

name: Fractional Shortening
description: Gives the percentage change in left ventricular diameter with each beat, a simple measure of systolic function.
notes: Normal is about 25–45 %.

name: Left Ventricular Stroke Work Index
description: Gives the work the left ventricle does per beat per square metre of body surface.
notes: Normal is about 50–62 g·m/m².

name: Change in Serum Sodium per Litre of Infusate (Adrogué–Madias)
description: Estimates how much one litre of an intravenous fluid will change serum sodium (Adrogué and Madias 2000).
notes: Limit correction of chronic hyponatraemia to about 8–10 mmol/L per day.

name: Expected Bicarbonate in Respiratory Acidosis
description: Gives the bicarbonate expected from renal and buffer compensation of respiratory acidosis.
notes: A measured value outside this suggests a second disorder.

name: Osmolal Gap
description: Gives the difference between measured and calculated osmolality; above about 10 suggests unmeasured osmoles such as toxic alcohols.
notes: Add ethanol/3.7 to the calculation if present.

name: Maximum Allowable Blood Loss
description: Estimates how much blood can be lost before reaching a transfusion threshold (simple formula used in anaesthesia).
notes: The exponential (log) version gives slightly larger values.

name: Red Cell Transfusion Volume (Paediatric)
description: Estimates the volume of packed red cells to raise a child's haemoglobin by a target amount (about 4 mL/kg per 1 g/dL).
notes: Some guidelines use 5 mL/kg per g/dL.

name: Gestational Age from Crown–Rump Length (Robinson)
description: Dates an early pregnancy from ultrasound crown–rump length (Robinson and Fleming 1975).
notes: Most accurate between about 7 and 13 weeks.

name: Growth z-Score from LMS Parameters
description: Converts a child's measurement into a z-score with the LMS parameters from WHO or CDC growth tables (Cole 1990).
notes: Look up L, M and S for the child's age and sex.

name: Urine Output Rate
description: Gives urine output normalised to body weight; below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours meets the KDIGO criterion for acute kidney injury.
notes: Children and infants have higher normal values.

name: Insulin Sensitivity Factor (1800 Rule)
description: Estimates how far one unit of rapid-acting insulin lowers blood glucose; use 100 instead of 1800 for mmol/L.
notes: A starting estimate to refine with glucose records.

name: Insulin-to-Carbohydrate Ratio (500 Rule)
description: Estimates how many grams of carbohydrate one unit of rapid-acting insulin covers.
notes: A starting estimate; individual ratios vary by time of day.

name: Insulin Correction Dose
description: Gives the rapid-acting insulin needed to bring a high glucose down to target.
notes: Subtract insulin still active from earlier doses.

name: Heart Rate from ECG Large Squares
description: Estimates heart rate from a standard ECG at 25 mm/s: 300 divided by the number of large squares between beats.
notes: Use 1500 ÷ small squares for more precision.

name: Paediatric Tracheal Tube Depth at the Lips
description: Estimates how deep a child's tracheal tube should sit at the lips: about three times its internal diameter.
notes: Confirm position clinically and with capnography.

name: Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio
description: Gives a simple inflammation marker from a blood count; high values are linked to worse outcomes in many diseases.
notes: Healthy adults are roughly 1–3.

name: BUN-to-Creatinine Ratio
description: Helps distinguish pre-renal causes (above about 20) from intrinsic kidney disease (10–20).
notes: GI bleeding and steroids also raise it.

name: Albumin-to-Globulin Ratio
description: Compares albumin with the other serum proteins; low values suggest liver disease, inflammation or myeloma.
notes: Normal is about 1.1–2.5.

name: Iron Deficit (Ganzoni)
description: Estimates the total iron needed to correct anaemia and refill stores (Ganzoni 1970), used to plan intravenous iron.
notes: Many centres now use simplified fixed-dose tables.

name: Intraocular Lens Power (SRK Formula)
description: Estimates the lens implant power for emmetropia after cataract surgery (Sanders, Retzlaff and Kraff 1980).
notes: Modern formulas (SRK/T, Barrett) are more accurate outside average eyes.

name: Spherical Equivalent of a Prescription
description: Gives the single average power of a spectacle prescription with astigmatism.
notes: Used to classify myopia and for contact lens fitting.

name: Vertex Distance Compensation
description: Converts spectacle lens power to the power needed at the eye (e.g. for contact lenses).
notes: Matters above about ±4 D.

name: Starting Total Daily Insulin Dose (Weight-Based)
description: Gives a common weight-based starting estimate for total daily insulin in type 2 diabetes or basal–bolus regimens.
notes: Adjust to glucose readings; lower doses for the elderly or kidney disease.

name: Pulse Pressure Variation

variables.label: Maximum pulse pressure over a breath
Minimum pulse pressure over a breath

description: Gives the respiratory variation of arterial pulse pressure in a ventilated patient; above about 13 % predicts fluid responsiveness.
notes: Valid only with controlled ventilation, regular rhythm and adequate tidal volume.

name: ROX Index
description: Predicts success of high-flow nasal oxygen: 4.88 or more at 12 hours suggests intubation will not be needed (Roca 2019).
notes: Lower values call for close reassessment.

name: Oxygen Saturation Index
description: A non-invasive substitute for the oxygenation index using SpO₂ instead of arterial PaO₂, used in paediatric ARDS.
notes: Valid when SpO₂ is 97 % or less.

name: Shunt Fraction (Qs/Qt)
description: Gives the fraction of cardiac output that bypasses ventilated lung (the shunt equation).
notes: Normal is below about 5 %.

name: Pulmonary-to-Systemic Flow Ratio (Qp/Qs)
description: Estimates the size of an intracardiac shunt from oxygen saturations at cardiac catheterisation.
notes: Above about 1.5 usually needs closure.

name: Sokolow–Lyon Voltage (LVH)

variables.label: Tallest R in V5 or V6

description: Adds ECG voltages to screen for left ventricular hypertrophy (Sokolow and Lyon 1949): 35 mm or more is positive.
notes: Specific but not very sensitive.

name: Cornell Voltage (LVH)
description: Screens for left ventricular hypertrophy on ECG: above 28 mm in men or 20 mm in women.
notes: More sensitive than Sokolow–Lyon in women.

name: Mentzer Index
description: Helps tell thalassaemia trait (below 13) from iron deficiency (above 13) in microcytic anaemia (Mentzer 1973).
notes: Confirm with haemoglobin electrophoresis and iron studies.

name: Castelli Risk Index I (TC/HDL)
description: Gives the total-to-HDL cholesterol ratio, a simple cardiovascular risk marker; below about 4.5 (men) or 4.0 (women) is desirable.
notes: Unit-independent, so mmol/L works too.

name: eGFR from Cystatin C (CKD-EPI 2012)
description: Estimates kidney function from cystatin C, which is less affected by muscle mass than creatinine (Inker 2012).
notes: Combined creatinine–cystatin equations are more accurate still.

name: Glucose Infusion Rate
description: Gives the glucose delivered in mg/kg/min, the standard way to prescribe dextrose for newborns.
notes: Neonates usually need 4–8 mg/kg/min.

name: Stroke Volume Variation

variables.label: Maximum stroke volume over a breath
Minimum stroke volume over a breath

description: Gives the respiratory variation in stroke volume in a ventilated patient; above about 10–12 % suggests fluid responsiveness.
notes: Same caveats as pulse pressure variation.

name: SpO₂/FiO₂ Ratio
description: Gives the SpO₂/FiO₂ ratio, a non-invasive surrogate for PaO₂/FiO₂; about 315 corresponds to P/F 300 and 235 to P/F 200 (Rice 2007).
notes: Unreliable when SpO₂ is above 97 %.
